evidence.field: 字形演變; Unicode; Han Yu Da Zidian reference
evidence.text: The character page identifies 衣 as U+8863 and labels examples from oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo and silk, seal-script, and Shuowen traditions. Its account says the ancient form depicts clothing with overlapping front lapels. The page labels a bronze example 集成02837 and cites 金文詁林索引8.252; the extracted text does not provide specimen-level dates.
evidence.title: 漢字「衣」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析; 形義通解; cited bronze inscription readings
evidence.text: The database analyzes oracle-bone and bronze 衣 as an upper garment, with collar, sleeves, and overlapping lapels visible. It says oracle-bone uses include place, personal, and sacrificial names; bronze inscriptions include the upper-garment use in 無叀鼎 (“賜汝玄衣”), a use read as 卒 in [冬戈]簋, and a disputed reading 通讀為殷 for 衣祀 in 天亡簋. These loan readings are inscription-specific and do not establish separate word etymologies. It also quotes the Shuowen explanation: 衣，依也。上曰衣，下曰裳。象覆二人之形。
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—衣

evidence.field: 字形流變; 字形解說; 字音及字義
evidence.text: The page presents oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal, and standard forms. It describes the early graph’s top as a collar and lower portions as sleeves and lapels, interpreting the whole as a frontal pictograph of an ancient garment whose sides overlap. It separately lists noun yi1 衣服 and verb yi4 穿衣服, without establishing their chronology or a derivational account.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 衣

evidence.text: The page provides a graphic sequence from oracle-bone and bronze through Chu manuscripts and seal script to the Shuowen form. It does not explain individual stroke changes or document corruption; its extracted commentary gives the overlapping-lapels interpretation. The page does not supply dates for each pictured form in the accessible text.
evidence.title: 漢字「衣」：字形演變

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.field: article discussion of 大豊（禮）簋 inscription
evidence.text: The article reports competing readings of the graph in 天亡簋: it is generally read as 衣 and often as 殷, while Liu Xinyuan and Li Xueqin instead read it as 卒. Its author accepts 卒, interpreting 卒祀 as completing the rite to Heaven. Thus this is not secure evidence that the garment word 衣 meant “rite” or that the graph was borrowed for 殷; the reading and sentence division are disputed.
evidence.title: 裘錫圭：大豊（禮）簋銘新釋

evidence.field: article abstract, interpretation of 天亡簋
evidence.text: A modern interpretation reads the phrase 衣祀于王 as describing King Wu carrying the ancestral shrine tablet on campaign to sacrifice to King Wen. This materially differs from readings that take 衣 as a loan for 殷 or as 卒. The article abstract supports reporting the disagreement, but does not by itself settle the graph reading.
evidence.title: 天亡簋铭文释义补苴

evidence.field: collection description; 天亡簋 inscription transcription
evidence.text: The museum’s object record reproduces a transcription of the early Western Zhou 天亡簋 inscription, including 衣祀于王. This corroborates that the phrase occurs in the transmitted transcription, but the object described is a modern calligraphic fan based on the inscription, not the ancient vessel itself, and the record does not resolve the phrase’s interpretation.
evidence.title: 天亡簋金文扇面-國立歷史博物館-藏品資料-101-00009

evidence.text: The page labels 天亡簋 as an early Western Zhou vessel and presents multiple transcriptions, all including a form transcribed as 衣祀于王, while varying in segmentation and neighboring graphs. It illustrates why the phrase’s reading should remain unsettled; the page is a text/transcription resource, not a direct inspection of the original vessel.
evidence.title: 天亡簋铭文

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi text quoted in CUHK database
evidence.text: The Han-period dictionary’s account says 衣 means 依, distinguishes upper 衣 from lower 裳, and explains the form as “象覆二人之形.” Treat this as the Shuowen author’s historical analysis, not independent confirmation of the pictograph’s origin; the consulted paleographic databases instead describe a garment with collar, sleeves, and overlapping lapels.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—衣

evidence.field: 衣 详细解释; yī and yì entries with cited literary examples
evidence.text: The modern dictionary lists upper garment, clothing generally, object-covering, moss, coating, and membrane as noun senses, and “wear/put on” and “cover/wrap” as verb senses. It cites early canonical texts for clothing and wearing (including 詩 and 孟子), but these later literary examples do not date the senses’ origin. The graphic extension from garment to cover/coating/membrane is semantically plausible, but this source does not establish a dated chain for each extension.
evidence.title: 衣 yī、yì - 汉典

evidence.field: Baxter-Sagart OC and MC entries; table PDF p. 122
evidence.text: The published table gives 衣 yī ‘clothes’: Middle Chinese 'j+j, Old Chinese *ʔ(r)əj; and 衣 yì ‘wear (v.t.)’: Middle Chinese 'j+jH, Old Chinese *ʔ(r)əj-s. The contrast supports a possible morphological relationship with *-s on the verb in this reconstruction, but reconstruction alone does not prove when or how the verb arose. Local table cross-check: sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv rows 4135 and 4190 contain the same MC and OC notations for the two 衣 entries. This local row is a check, not an independent phonological proof.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

evidence.source: Local Unihan_Readings.txt row for 衣; upstream Unicode Unihan page could not be inspected
evidence.text: The provided local exact row records kMandarin yī for 衣. I attempted the official Unicode click-through record for U+8863, but the page was inaccessible through the web tool. Accordingly this local row is reported as local metadata only, not as verified external evidence. Mandarin yī is current pronunciation metadata and does not establish an ancient sound relationship.
evidence.title: Unicode Unihan record for U+8863 (attempted; inaccessible)

evidence.field: published MC/OC row for 衣; compare local sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv rows 4135 and 4190
evidence.text: The local TSV has two rows for 衣 and agrees with the inspected published table’s readings: yī, MC 'j+j, OC *ʔ(r)əj, ‘clothes’; and yì, MC 'j+jH, OC *ʔ(r)əj-s, ‘wear (v.t.)’. The parenthesized (r) is uncertain in this system. These are separate lexical readings of the same graph; the table alone cannot date semantic extension or prove a derivational chronology.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

gaps: No inspected primary glyph image was visually assessed in this research. The character-development sequence and pictographic analysis rely on database descriptions, not this researcher’s visual inspection.

The accessible paleographic descriptions do not date individual oracle-bone/bronze specimens precisely, and the Academia Sinica extracted page lacks dates for each form. A precise earliest graphic attestation date remains unverified.

The earliest oracle-bone uses reported by CUHK are proper/place/sacrificial-name uses, not clearly garment-noun contexts. Earliest attested garment noun is therefore not established by the consulted evidence; a dated bronze garment use is reported for 無叀鼎, but its absolute date was not independently verified here.

The chronology and semantic pathway from ‘upper garment’ to clothing generally, cover, skin/coating, and membrane are not demonstrated by dated evidence in the inspected sources. These are separately recorded dictionary senses, not a proven linear semantic history.
The phrase 衣祀 in 天亡簋 has materially competing readings: 殷, 卒, or a distinct ritual interpretation. The exact graph reading, sentence division, and interpretation remain unresolved.

Baxter–Sagart’s noun/verb contrast supports an analysis with an OC *-s suffix on yì ‘wear’, but the consulted evidence does not independently date the verb or prove the direction and chronology of noun-to-verb derivation.

The Wiktionary-derived Proto-Sino-Tibetan *w(y)a-t ~ wit comparison and Burmese ဝတ် were not independently verified from an accessible primary comparative source. Baxter–Sagart *ʔ(r)əj does not by itself establish the Chinese word’s relationship to that proposed cognate set; sound correspondence and semantic history remain gaps.
